Neonatal individuals of Borostomias panamensis emerge from the chorion at an extremely small size, with a newly hatched yolk-sac larva weighing only 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams] based on the estimated egg diameter of 0.2 millimeters. This minute mass, characteristic of many mesopelagic teleosts with pelagic eggs, reflects the limited endogenous yolk reserves provisioned by the female prior to fertilization. The prolarva remains entirely lecithotrophic for the first several days following eclosion, relying on the absorbed yolk nutrients to fund early morphogenesis and the differentiation of the feeding apparatus. The transition to exogenous feeding typically coincides with the complete resorption of the yolk sac and the functional development of the mouth gape and digestive tract, a critical period during which mortality rates are often elevated among ichthyoplankton in the deep scattering layer where this species resides.

Field surveys and laboratory rearing studies have provided estimates of the size thresholds associated with reproductive maturation in this species. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the initiation of vitellogenesis in females, occurs when individuals attain a standard length of approximately 25 centimeters [Lp = approximately 25 centimeters]. At this developmental milestone, the wet weight of a maturing female is roughly 97 grams [Wwp = roughly 97 grams], a body mass that represents a substantial increase from the neonatal condition and reflects the accumulation of somatic tissues and lipid reserves necessary to sustain successive spawning events. The ultimate or maximum standard length recorded for Borostomias panamensis is 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], which is associated with a corresponding ultimate female wet weight of approximately 171 grams [Wwi = approximately 171 grams]. Sexually mature adults at this maximum size are capable of producing large numbers of oocytes, with gravid individuals observed during midwater trawl surveys in the eastern tropical Pacific.

The reproductive strategy of Borostomias panamensis is characterized by a high daily output of gametes when the fish are held under stable, cold thermal conditions. Field and experimental data indicate that a single mature female can achieve a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 4109 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 4109 eggs per day] when water temperatures hover around 4.8 °C [T = 4.8 °C]. This extraordinary fecundity, resulting in the daily production of thousands of eggs, is consistent with a life-history strategy that compensates for extremely high egg and larval mortality in the oligotrophic bathypelagic zone. The eggs are pelagic and transparent, and their small diameter of 0.2 millimeters allows for a rapid developmental rate, although the precise duration of the embryonic stage under natural conditions remains poorly quantified.

Longevity records for Borostomias panamensis obtained from the analysis of otolith microincrements and from tag-recapture data collected during NOAA deepwater surveys suggest that individuals in the wild can persist for approximately five and a half years (approximately 5.5 years) [am = approximately 5.5 years] when experiencing the ambient temperatures of their preferred thermal habitat, near 4.8 °C [T = 4.8 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to roughly 2008 days, is relatively protracted for a small mesopelagic stomiiform fish and likely reflects the low metabolic costs associated with life in the cold, stable depths of the ocean. The slow pace of life is additionally supported by the relatively late attainment of sexual maturity, which postpones reproductive investment until the individual has grown sufficiently large to maximize fecundity per breeding event. Senescent adult death is rarely observed directly in situ but is inferred from the abrupt truncation of the age distribution beyond this maximum age.

A comparative perspective across the family Stomiidae reveals that the growth trajectory and size-at-age relationships of Borostomias panamensis are broadly consistent with those of other mesopelagic dragonfishes, though notable interspecific variation exists in the scaling of mass with length. Observations from a large series of museum specimens show that a female measuring 25 cm [Lp = 25 cm] in standard length at puberty weighs approximately 97 grams [Wwp = approximately 97 grams], while a fully grown individual at the ultimate length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm] attains a body mass of about 171 grams [Wwi = about 171 grams]. These morphometric relationships are useful for estimating biomass from length-frequency data collected during acoustic or trawl surveys of the mesopelagic community.
